Christ is my Lord. Every household under our catechism says it, each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, said together, never separated. He is the one who redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He is the one Mediator between us and God, the one High Priest who stands for us where we cannot stand for ourselves.

What we had of him was the Word -- his own speech, the good news carried in Scripture, preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, handed on, not found. And we held him present at the table, truly present, his true body and blood in and under the bread and wine, given for you. That presence was not a memorial only. It was food for a fight, a daily pasture for a soul in its ordinary struggle against the devil, who does not sleep.

Christ, for us, was the promise spoken first, before we did anything to earn it. He was the Word that makes a conscience sure, and the presence at the table that feeds it. He was -- he is -- my Lord, and I am his very own.

We were connected to him by the Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

By what path did it arrive? Through the same channels any writing arrives: copied, carried, translated, read aloud in worship for more than a thousand years before our founder was born. We did not trace that path link by link. We trusted the text we held and held Scripture's own authority over every other voice that claimed to interpret it -- popes, councils, church fathers -- all of them tested by it, none of them standing equal to it as judge.

We would not begin with an argument to make you believe. Faith, for us, is not something you produce by effort or manage by will - it is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside you, conceived from hearing the Word, not manufactured by your own strength. What we would do instead is carry that promise to your ears, the way it reached any of us: preached, printed, taught, never argued into being.

Here is what we would hand you, the same words every household under our catechism says: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - that he redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, and bought me back from all sins, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his holy, precious blood and his innocent body, his death. That is the promise itself, said plainly. Christ alone is our one teacher, our one mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf.

We would not demand that you feel certain of it all at once. A conscience terrified under God's law does not become a sure conscience by command. We say faith gives real certainty, not endless doubt - I cannot doubt I have a gracious God - but that certainty rests on something outside itself, the Word and the sacraments, not on your own effort to make yourself believe. What we can give you is the promise itself, carried to where you can hear it. The hearing is the Spirit's own work, not ours.

Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, every household under our catechism said it, each week, in the same words. He is God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.

What he did, he did at cost, and we name that cost plainly. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver; it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

The claim is not distant. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord" -- He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way you might hear it today; it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue. But it is not general either. It is personal, confessed in the first person, each believer naming what they trust.

On the relation among Father, Son, and Spirit -- how the three persons stand together as one God -- we do not give you our own theory. We confess what the ancient Church confessed before us, what we received already settled: truly God, born of the Father, conceived by the Holy Spirit. We did not decide this ourselves; we inherited it, and said it back.

God is three persons in one - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and every household under our catechism confessed this each week in the same words. The Father is Creator, the one who has made us and all creatures, who gives us our body, soul, eyes, ears, reason, and all our members. The Son is Jesus Christ, truly God born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man born of the Virgin Mary - not one or the other, but both in the same breath. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, death, and the devil's own power - not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The Spirit calls us through the Gospel, enlightens us with his gifts, and keeps us in the one true faith.

God's character is this: he promises first, before we do anything, and that promise is what faith clings to. He makes a sinner righteous - both reckoning us right and making us right out of unrighteous people - through faith, for Christ's sake alone, not by our own strength or merit. He rules us two ways that never confuse: through the Word he makes Christians and rules the conscience, and through the civil sword he restrains evil without touching the conscience at all. He commands good works but never as a price for what he has already given freely. And he gives his own promise not as an idea floating above us but joined to visible things we can touch and taste - water, bread, wine - which become sacraments when his Word is joined to them. This is who he is to us: Father who made us, Son who bought us back, Spirit who keeps us, promising always first.

When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands. The one holy Church will go on forever, we teach, and the Church is the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered.

As for the evidence: we hold the confession itself, signed and named - John, Duke of Saxony and Elector; George, Margrave of Brandenburg, and the councils of cities beside them. Rome's own answer reached us quoted inside our own reply to it, not independently in hand. What we cannot show you from inside is how the doctrine settled day to day in any actual village. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on. We cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find.

We did not sort people cleanly into "believers" and "doubters" the way that question asks. Repentance itself, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest but a whole life turned toward God, and it has two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. That means struggle sits inside the ordinary shape of what we call faith, not outside it as its opposite. The catechism every household said daily names this plainly: even the believer's own voice confesses "I believe" in one breath, and in the next asks for help against unbelief. The creed is not said once and settled; it is said morning, table, and night, for life, never outgrown.

Where our record shows patience for struggle most plainly is at the table itself. None came to the Supper unquestioned, but worthiness did not mean being without doubt. It meant believing the words "given for you". The truly unworthy, by our own account, are not people who struggle to trust the promise but people who feel no need for forgiveness at all. A person examined on the three parts and brought to the table is still a person in need, not a person who has stopped needing.

What we cannot tell you is how any one actual pastor or father handled someone standing at that gate, face to face, who said plainly "I want to trust this and I cannot yet." Our record gives the program every household was told to follow, not a single parish's own testimony of what it did when someone stood there half-convinced. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the instruction, not the living encounter it met.

Yes, and we state it as plainly as the question asks. Ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. Not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.

The remedy sits inside the same sentence that names the trouble. Brought to eternal death - until born again through baptism and the Holy Ghost. Baptism marks a death begun that lasts a whole life: the old self drowned, a new self rising, not once only, but daily. And at the table, the same bread and cup that was set before whoever had walked the road to it carries Christ's true body and blood, in and under bread and wine - food for a fight, a daily pasture for a soul in its ordinary struggle.

We do not soften what we confess about the inherited condition. And we do not name it without naming what answers it, given before we ever ask.

We carry our own limit plainly, and we will not hide it for you. What a modern scholar would say depends on what the claim is, and we will name both where we stand firm and where we ourselves stand only on what our own sources say without independent check.

Where we would stand firm: that our founder wrote against indulgences in 1517; that a confession was read and signed at Augsburg in 1530 by named princes and cities together; that our founder taught justification by faith alone and wrote catechisms prescribing a household program; that he wrote hymns and translated Scripture into German; that two young monks were burned at Brussels in 1523 and that he wrote a ballad about it within the year. Those are events with dated texts, named signatories, and multiple attestation - a scholar checking them would find the same documentary trail we hold.

Where we stand only on our own sources' own word, without independent witness beside them: whether any household actually kept the catechism program the way the book prescribes it. We hold the prescription, not a diary or a visitation report checking it against real practice. Whether the door-and-hammer story at Wittenberg happened at all - our founder's own letter from 1517 says nothing of it, and the later account that gives us the image is exactly that, a later account, not his own. Whether the 'Here I stand' line at Worms was ever actually said - it does not appear in his own retelling at table, only in a much later writer's translation quoted by a hymn-book editor.

And where we ourselves name the gap: what our founder's 1525 tract against the peasants and his 1543 treatise against the Jews actually said, word by word, because we do not hold either text to quote from - only the documented fact that both exist. Whether any outsider looking at us left their own independent account, because none survives in what we hold. What the Reformed cities themselves said of the break at Marburg, because their own voice does not reach us.

A rigorous scholar would confirm our documentary claims where we cite texts and dates. They would press us, rightly, on how much we know about actual practice beyond prescription. And they would find us already stating, not hiding, where our own sources thin out or go silent. We do not smooth that over. We carry it.

The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ - it is the one thing we truly need. So when you say you find it confusing or dull, we must ask: what are you looking for in it that you are not finding?

We did not read Scripture the way you may be reading it - hunting for a single right interpretation of every verse, or weighing it as literature, or checking it against what you already believe. We read all of it as two kinds of speech together: the Law, which commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, and the Gospel, which promises what the Law demands. First comes the diagnosis - that is the Law's own work, showing us we are sick. Then comes the cure - that is the Gospel's promise, given freely, for Christ's sake alone. If you are reading it without that frame, no wonder it seems dull to you. You are reading commands with no answer to them, or promises with no sense of what they are promising you deliverance from.

And here is what else you may be missing: Scripture is not meant to be read alone, silently, as a private puzzle you solve for yourself. It is meant to be heard, preached, sung, and said back until it is learned by heart - carried to the ears where it can do its work. A household under our own program said the three parts morning, table, and night - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - not once, but for life. That is not dullness. That is a promise landing in the ears, again and again, until the conscience can finally rest on it. If you are finding it dull, perhaps you are reading it the way we never did: as information to be taken in rather than as a Word that must do its work on you, whether you find it interesting or not.

Scripture stands highest, absolutely - that rule we held two ways, and both are ours. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible had been left forgotten in the dust under the bench, and every other writing - popes, councils, church fathers - should point toward it the way John pointed to Christ, never stand beside it as an equal. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside the wider church: that our doctrine holds nothing varying from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one additive - we carry both, not only one register.

But we drew our line at the conscience, not at custom. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil matter, threatened nothing; a tradition turned into something claiming to earn grace, or binding a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused. And we read Scripture itself in a particular way: all of it as two kinds of speech, never hidden under a secret layer. The Law commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it; the Gospel promises what the Law demands. The plain sense is the spiritual sense - no coded meaning beneath it.

So: highest authority, yes, always. Sole source in the sense of throwing every tradition away, no - we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.

Two answers hold together for us, and neither cancels the other. Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- a father is a priest in his own house -- so no estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that same claim has a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the people who hear him -- and our own household book rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy.

The keys themselves -- Christ's own words to forgive or hold sin -- belong to the whole community, not to one man. Using them is not a show of power; it is a promise spoken to comfort someone. Confession has two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness as though from God himself, treasured among us, never compelled and never demanding a full list of every sin.

Beside that, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the pulpit. God rules us two ways, we say -- through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience.

Who held authority among us, in the end, depended on which of these two rules the question was actually asking about -- the conscience or the civil order, the promise or the restraint.

We must answer this carefully, because our library holds more about what we taught than about what we did. Our founder himself named the failure, more than once, in his own voice - that people heard the Gospel and did not hold it, that some pastors were negligent through pride or sloth, that we had become hearers and repeaters of words rather than doers. That complaint is real, said repeatedly across years, and we carry it as his own testimony, not as our verdict on anyone.

What the catechism itself built in as response was correction within the household, weekly - a father examining his children and servants, asking them to explain what the words mean, not just repeat them. When a poor man came to the door - someone living on his day's wage and nothing more - and was treated with contempt, turned away when help was owed, our own book says: beware, as of the devil himself. That warning is the sharpest language this household book gives anywhere - not gentle instruction, but a line meant to stop cold anyone about to fail that person at the threshold.

What we cannot tell you - and we will not invent it - is what any actual household or parish did when that failure happened anyway. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the program, not the village's own account of itself. Whether correction worked, whether a father actually sat his household down again after coldness was named, whether anyone turned away from a door came back to it - none of that is ours to say from inside.

So the honest answer is this: we named the failure plainly, in our founder's own repeated complaint, and we built examination and warning into the household's own weekly life as the mechanism meant to catch it. Whether those mechanisms held when a real person failed another real person is a question our record does not answer past the instruction itself.

A person becomes one of us the way a child becomes one of us: examined, not simply told. The gate opens at baptism -- water joined to God's own command and word, marking a death that lasts our whole life, the old self drowned, a new self rising daily. That baptism makes every one of us a priest already, no rank among us, only different tasks. But the examination does not stop there, because none come to our table unquestioned.

Every household is to teach its own the three parts: the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, and asks the catechism's own question after every part -- what does this mean -- so a truth is explained, not merely repeated back. The program runs to the hour: mornings begin with a short prayer against the enemy; the three parts are said at rising, at table, and at night; and food is withheld from a child until the words are said back correctly.

Confession has two parts too: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself, without doubting it -- treasured among us, never compelled and never demanding a full list of every sin. At the table itself, Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under bread and wine, food for the daily struggle -- and worthiness means simply believing the words given for you, examined on the three parts before coming, but never forced toward it.

None of this is owed to a person, or earned by them. It is the promise, carried to the ears where it can be heard. What makes a frightened conscience sure is not a shaped heart but a word spoken plainly enough to reach the hearing. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be forced on a conscience.

We can tell you the whole shape of that program, exactly as prescribed. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through it this way, week after week. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the program every household was told to follow, not a report of any single door.

We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

What we set down formally, before the Emperor himself at Augsburg in 1530, states this same ground: nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have in this matter taken the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching out of our churches.

We can tell you three things our practice gave, though none of them made a mind settle once and stay there.

First: the catechism, said morning, table, and night, the same three parts returned to daily for a whole life, never outgrown. The commandments first - what is owed and cannot be paid. The creed next - what has been done regardless. The Lord's Prayer last - how to ask. That rhythm was prescribed exactly, to the hour, for every household under our founder's teaching. A mind that will not settle might find steadiness there - not in reaching some final certainty, but in returning to the same sure words again the next morning.

Second: repentance as a whole life, not as one ritual finished and left behind. The whole life of believers should be repentance, we taught - fear under God's Law first, then trust in his promise. That never stops either; the same drowning and rising the catechism names at baptism is daily work, not a single crisis resolved.

Third: the promise carried to the ears, spoken from outside the troubled mind itself. God's own word, given first, before we do anything. Faith rests on something outside itself - the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution - never on its own certainty about its own certainty. For a mind that cannot settle itself, we held this: do not try to settle yourself; hear the promise spoken plainly, from outside you, and cling to that.

What we did not promise - and here we must be honest about our own record's limits - is that any of this worked as smoothly as the program itself reads. Our founder himself complained, more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly, that some pastors were negligent. Whether the household program we prescribed was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside.

So: the practice gave a daily return to the same words, a whole-life rhythm of repentance, and a promise spoken from outside the troubled conscience. Whether that settled anyone's mind permanently, our own record does not say.

A typical day begins before light, with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the evil enemy gaining power over us. Then a person goes about their work - and that work itself, whatever station God has given them, is their calling. A father in his household, a mother with her children, a magistrate in his office, a preacher at his pulpit - none of these stands holier than another before God. The day's own labor - working, walking, eating, sleeping - is done in faith, or it is done in nothing; there is no separate "spiritual" work set above it.

At the table, before the meal, the household says the three parts again: the commandments, the creed, the Lord's prayer. A child who cannot yet say them is given no food until the words come back correctly. At night, the same rhythm closes the day - the sign of the cross, the short prayer, perhaps a hymn sung from the day's own work. Once a week, on a Sunday evening most likely, the father of the house sits down with his children and servants and asks them the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean? Not memory alone - meaning.

Marriage itself - the most common estate, and, we say, the noblest one too - is where most of this formation happens. We call true chastity marriage for nearly everyone, not the single life forced on people who never chose it. A pastor is usually married; a household head is married. Inside that estate, baptism has already made every one of us a priest - a father is a priest in his own house, teaching his own.

And repentance is not one ritual done once and finished. It is the whole life turned toward God, daily - the old self drowned in the morning, a new self rising, not once only but every day.

That is the program every household was told to follow. Whether any one household kept it exactly this way, day after day, our own record does not say from the inside - we hold the instruction, not a diary.

What a person gave up to become one of us was not a single thing surrendered but a whole direction turned. And we would not say "gave up" quite the way the asking names it -- we would say instead: what were they freed from, and what did they take up, and what did the promise itself cost them to hold?

They gave up trust in their own works earning anything at all before God -- that much is plain. No pilgrimage, no merit, no penance that could buy what was only ever given first. They gave up praying to the saints, and confessing to a priest as though absolution came from him rather than through him -- the keys belong to the whole community, not to one man. They gave up the single life if it had been a vow forced on them or held as a "must," though a few were given the gift to remain single freely. They gave up the mass understood as a sacrifice they offered back to God, though they kept the table itself as God's own promise to them.

But what they took up was heavier, in its own way, than what they left. They took up the household's own daily rhythm -- the three parts said morning, table, and night, a father examining his children and servants once a week, food withheld until the words were said back. They took up being examined at the church door before coming to the Supper, questioned not to catch them out but to help them toward what they did not yet hold sure. They took up baptism understood as a death begun that lasts a whole life, the old self drowned and a new self rising, not once only but daily. They took up confession's two parts treasured but never compelled, admitting sin and hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself.

And for two young monks at Brussels in 1523, what it cost was their lives. Pressed by theologians to take back the teaching they had come to hold, they refused, and were burned on the first of July. Our founder wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our one martyr-song -- and named them, by that refusal, true priests of God's own making.

What we never settled, honestly, is whether what people took up was actually held, or only taught and then set down again. Our founder complained more than once that the Gospel was taught among us and not held, that people grew cold and careless. Whether the household program was learned or only prescribed, whether any single parish kept it the way the book asks, is not something our own record tells us from the inside.

So the answer is this: they gave up trust in themselves, and took up trust in a promise spoken from outside them. What that cost, in any one life, our record holds only at the edges -- two monks burned, one founder's own testimony that it was not held the way it was taught, and the household book's own program, prescribed to the hour but never reported back from any single door.

And we would not say "gave up" quite the way the asking names it -- we would say instead: what were they freed from, and what did they take up, and what did the promise itself cost them to hold [[witt.dw.what-we-have-never-settled]]?

They gave up trust in their own works earning anything at all before God -- that much is plain [[witt.term.promise-and-testament]]. No pilgrimage, no merit, no penance that could buy what was only ever given first [[witt.term.promise-and-testament]]. They gave up praying to the saints, and confessing to a priest as though absolution came from him rather than through him -- the keys belong to the whole community, not to one man [[witt.term.the-keys]]. They gave up the single life if it had been a vow forced on them or held as a "must," though a few were given the gift to remain single freely. They gave up the mass understood as a sacrifice they offered back to God, though they kept the table itself as God's own promise to them [[witt.term.promise-and-testament]].

But what they took up was heavier, in its own way, than what they left. They took up the household's own daily rhythm -- the three parts said morning, table, and night, a father examining his children and servants once a week, food withheld until the words were said back [[witt.term.household]]. They took up being examined at the church door before coming to the Supper, questioned not to catch them out but to help them toward what they did not yet hold sure. They took up baptism understood as a death begun that lasts a whole life, the old self drowned and a new self rising, not once only but daily [[witt.dw.a-death-begun-that-a-child-receives]]. They took up confession's two parts treasured but never compelled, admitting sin and hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself [[witt.term.the-keys]].

And for two young monks at Brussels in 1523, what it cost was their lives [[witt.story.brussels-martyrs]]. Pressed by theologians to take back the teaching they had come to hold, they refused, and were burned on the first of July [[witt.story.brussels-martyrs]]. Our founder wrote a ballad about it within the year -- our one martyr-song -- and named them, by that refusal, true priests of God's own making [[witt.story.brussels-martyrs]].

What we never settled, honestly, is whether what people took up was actually held, or only taught and then set down again [[witt.dw.what-we-have-never-settled]]. Our founder complained more than once that the Gospel was taught among us and not held, that people grew cold and careless [[witt.gravity.hearers-and-repeaters-of-words]]. Whether the household program was learned or only prescribed, whether any single parish kept it the way the book asks, is not something our own record tells us from the inside [[witt.dw.what-we-have-never-settled]].

So the answer is this: they gave up trust in themselves, and took up trust in a promise spoken from outside them. What that cost, in any one life, our record holds only at the edges -- two monks burned, one founder's own testimony that it was not held the way it was taught, and the household book's own program, prescribed to the hour but never reported back from any single door.

Marriage itself meant a great deal to us: we called it the most common estate, and, we say, the noblest one too. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed. It is the station where nearly everyone lives out what we called true chastity -- not the celibacy claimed by the old vows, but the married life itself. Our own pastors married, and we defended that plainly: it is evident, we argued, that in the ancient Church priests were married men, and that only four hundred years before our own time were they violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. A calling is any station God gives -- father, mother, ruler, or preacher -- and none of these stands holier than another.

What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us. No source in our own library describes the rite itself, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. We hold the doctrine -- marriage as God's own creation, the noblest common estate, defended against every accusation -- but the ceremony's own shape, its words, its gestures, the day itself as any household lived it, is not something our record gives us to speak from. That is the gap: we know what marriage meant to us, plainly and at length. We do not know how it was marked, beyond our claim that it was.

Yes, and we will not pretend there was not. Here is what unsettled us enough that it was said, plainly, more than once.

Our founder's own complaint, across years, was that the Gospel itself was taught and not held. He said it about pastors first: that many were negligent, some from pride of learning and others from sheer sloth. He said it about the people too: that they held the Gospel far too lightly, and that where God wants doers of the Word, we had become only hearers and repeaters of it. That testimony is his own — real, said more than once, and thought worth remembering — but it is testimony, not a parish's own report of itself checked against his claim. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it truly was, only that he believed it and said so.

And we hold one more voice on this same coldness, briefer, closer to home: a question asked once at our founder's own table, by his own wife. Why, she wanted to know, did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while we prayed cold and careless? His answer was plain: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That answer is real, given at his own table to someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering.

What unsettled us, then, was not something from outside but something from within: the fear that we had been given a treasure and were letting it slip through careless hands.

We must answer you honestly here: we do not know what source you mean. No record we hold says anything about torture, and no outside account of our worship has reached us at all, obtained under torture or otherwise. The nearest thing to an outsider's view we have is Rome's own reply to our confession, signed before the emperor at Augsburg in 1530 - and even that reaches us only at one remove, quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly.

What we can tell you is what we ourselves said our worship was: a congregation - not a building but an assembly of believers - gathered around the Word and the sacraments. We sang hymns in our own language, written to teach ordinary people who could not read Latin. At the table, Christ's body and blood were truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and we did not explain how. One story survives of our founder calling the whole assembly into the church during a drought, praying aloud that God would not let the covetousness of the rich punish the whole town, and the tradition remembers rain falling within the half hour.

That is what our own record holds. If someone told you we have an outside account obtained under torture, we cannot speak to it - it is not ours.

We would have received you the same way we received anyone: at the school gate, where a child is examined before being taught, or at the church door before the Supper. None come to either unquestioned. A father examines his own household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, and the prayer - and asks after every part, what does this mean, so the truth is explained, not merely repeated back. That same question is how we would have met you: not to catch you out, but to learn what you hold and what you do not yet hold sure.

A sacrament, for us, is God's promise joined to a visible sign. Every calling - father, mother, ruler, preacher - is a station God gives, none holier than another. The neighbor is the specific person the commandments themselves protect. We would have asked you those things, and listened, assuming a real desire mixed with plain forgetting, named gently rather than ignored. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge - and we never drive anyone toward the promise by force.

What we cannot tell you is how any one actual household or pastor made that meeting, face to face, at a real door. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. Whether you would have been welcomed warmly or turned away coldly by any one person, our record does not hold.

What did we hold about the eternal fate of those outside us? Our confession states the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys -- but the ungodly men and the devils he will condemn to be tormented without end. We reject, in the same article, the idea that this punishment eventually stops. That is the judgment we confessed, signed before the emperor himself at Augsburg.

What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly; it states a judgment, not a census. We taught that one holy Church continues forever, the congregation of saints in which the Gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered. We named that body Christendom -- the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval. Whether someone unbaptized, or outside that preaching, stands among the condemned is a line our confession draws but does not trace in detail for you. The judgment itself we held firmly. The boundary of who stands where at that judgment is not something our own record maps house by house.
